content: General Guidelines for Creating Chapters and Microchapters A chapter is a collection of smaller sections referred to as microchapters. For example, the chapter on Pericarditis may include microchapters such as Overview of Pericarditis, Pathophysiology of Pericarditis, and Treatment of Pericarditis. Microchapters are designed to allow users to efficiently access specific content and to optimize loading and display speeds, particularly on mobile devices. When structuring chapters and microchapters, it is essential to maintain consistency across the site. Each microchapter should begin with the same page name, such as Pericarditis Overview or Pericarditis Pathophysiology. Only the first word of each title should be capitalized. Additionally, all microchapters listed in the template on the right-hand side should be present on the main chapter's homepage. If certain titles in the template are irrelevant, they may be removed. For example, if there are no primary or secondary prevention strategies for a condition, such as pericarditis, the corresponding microchapter can be omitted. Navigation Box at the Top of the Page The navigation box is displayed only on the disease's homepage. If the image at the top of the page is illustrative, it can be retained or replaced with a copyleft image that better represents the condition. Links to external sources, such as eMedicine, should be removed. Synonyms and Keywords To enhance searchability, use Google to identify synonyms and alternative terms. Replace overused words with more specific terminology. For example, substitute about with regarding or give with administer. Related Chapters Avoid using the phrase see also to link related chapters, as it may create confusion about whether the linked chapters cover the same or similar topics. Instead, use the term Related chapters. Appropriate Copyleft Sources When including images or videos, ensure they are sourced from copyleft repositories such as the National Library of Medicine, Diseases Database, or Radiopaedia. Cite the original source even if the image is copyleft. If there is any uncertainty about the copyright status, consult with a knowledgeable individual, such as Dr. Gibson. Patient Information Page Overview The goal of the patient information page is to provide a concise summary of the condition, focusing on its diagnosis and treatment. This text will appear in Google searches and must be grammatically perfect. The content should include an overview of the disease's pathophysiology, epidemiology, common causes, prognosis, and a summary of diagnostic and treatment approaches. Historical Perspective This section provides background on the history of the disease, including its discovery, notable outbreaks, and key scientific advancements. It may also highlight landmark changes in the study or management of the condition. This section is not intended for patient history or natural history. Classification This section outlines any condition-specific classification systems, such as subcategories or ordinal levels of disease severity. It is an optional microchapter and should only be included if the content is substantial enough to warrant a dedicated page. Pathophysiology The pathophysiology section explains the biological mechanisms underlying the disease. This may include descriptions of embryological, molecular, or genetic abnormalities, as well as pathogenesis and pathology images. Copyleft images and videos should be used to illustrate these concepts. Causes This section provides a comprehensive list of potential underlying causes of the condition, categorized by organ system. It includes a complete differential diagnosis and should not be renamed as etiology. This section does not describe what the disease causes or how it is distinguished from other disorders; those topics are covered in separate chapters. Differentiating the Condition from Other Diseases This section provides a systematic approach to identifying other potential diseases with similar signs and symptoms. It includes guidance on interpreting physical examination findings, laboratory results, and diagnostic protocols. Commonly associated conditions and known exclusions should also be listed. Epidemiology and Demographics This section presents data on the determinants and distribution of the disease within a population. It includes information on at-risk populations (e.g., by gender, race, age, socioeconomic status, diet, geographic location, and environmental conditions) and measures such as incidence, prevalence, mortality, and morbidity. Potential biases in disease studies should also be addressed. Risk Factors This section identifies well-defined determinants of the disease, such as lifestyle habits, environmental exposures, and genetic characteristics. It is important to note that risk factors indicate correlation, not causation, which is covered in the Causes section. Screening The screening section provides an overview of methodologies used to detect the disease in asymptomatic individuals. It includes descriptions of tests, their sensitivity and specificity, and their advantages and disadvantages. Questions such as Why screen? and What diseases are appropriate for screening? should be addressed. Biases such as lead-time bias and overdiagnosis should also be discussed. Natural History, Complications, and Prognosis This section describes the natural progression of the disease without treatment, complications arising from the disease or its treatment, and anticipated outcomes for treated and untreated patients. It may include life expectancy projections and the potential need for re-treatment. History and Symptoms This section focuses on the symptoms verbalized by the patient, including common and less common symptoms, the rapidity of symptom onset, and links to related WikiDoc pages for further explanation. It does not include physical examination findings. Physical Examination This section lists symptoms observed during a physical examination, categorized by organ system (e.g., skin, eyes, heart, lungs). It may include differentiating characteristics that indicate disease severity. Patient-identifiable information should not be included in any images. Laboratory Findings This section summarizes relevant laboratory tests and findings, such as electrolyte levels, kidney and liver function tests, complete blood counts, and biopsies. Imaging studies are not included in this section. Imaging Studies Separate sections are dedicated to specific imaging modalities, such as electrocardiograms (EKG), chest X-rays, CT scans, and echocardiography. Each section includes indications, contraindications, advantages, disadvantages, and copyleft image examples. Patient-identifiable information must not be included in any images. Treatment The treatment section provides an overview of management strategies, including risk factor modification, pharmacological therapies, and surgical interventions. Treatment approaches may vary by condition, and microchapters should be created as needed. Categories Categories at the bottom of the WikiDoc article help organize content and allow readers to navigate related topics. Categories must follow sitewide conventions to avoid dead links or duplicated content. Examples include Category: Cardiology or Category: Physical Examination.
